summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) to show both sums vanish modulo \(p\) at indices \(p,\ldots,2p-2\); they also give \(a(p-1)=1\), while divisibility of central binomial coefficients leaves only \(k=(p-1)/2\) in \(c(p-1)\), yielding \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Reversing the columns of each Hankel matrix then makes it triangular with constant diagonal value at \(p-1\), and the reversal sign \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), together with \(x^p=x\) modulo \(p\), gives the two determinant congruences.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                  \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and perform all calculations below in the field
\(\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\). We will first establish the binomial congruences needed for the two sequences, then prove their relevant values and vanishings, and finally evaluate the determinants.

## 1. Binomial congruences

We use the one-digit form of Lucas's theorem:
\[
\binom nk\equiv
 \binom{n\bmod p}{k\bmod p}\binom{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}{\lfloor k/p\rfloor}
 \pmod p.
\]
In every application below, the quotients are small enough that this single step gives all the information needed.

If \(0\le m,k<p\), Lucas's theorem gives
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv \binom mk,                                      \tag{1}
\]
because the base-\(p\) digits involved are \((1,m)\) and \((0,k)\). Likewise, if \(0\le m,j<p\), then
\[
\binom{p+m}{p+j}\equiv \binom mj,                                    \tag{2}
\]
since the corresponding digits are \((1,m)\) and \((1,j)\).

We also need two facts about central binomial coefficients. First, if
\[
p\le 2k\quad\hbox{and}\quad k<p,
\]
then
\[
\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0.                                                 \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, \(2k<2p\), so the low base-\(p\) digit of \(2k\) is \(2k-p\), whereas that of \(k\) is \(k\). Since \(2k-p<k\), Lucas's theorem contains the zero factor \(\binom{2k-p}{k}\).

Second, for every \(0\le r<p\),
\[
\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\equiv 2\binom{2r}{r}.                              \tag{4}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2r<p\), then the base-\(p\) digits of \(2(p+r)=2p+2r\) are \((2,2r)\), and those of \(p+r\) are \((1,r)\). Thus Lucas gives
\[
\binom{2(p+r)}{p+r}\equiv \binom21\binom{2r}{r}
=2\binom{2r}{r}.
\]
If \(2r\ge p\), then (3) shows that \(\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0\). On the left, the low digit of \(2(p+r)=3p+(2r-p)\) is \(2r-p<r\), so Lucas likewise shows that the left side is zero. This proves (4) in both cases.

Finally, for \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.                                          \tag{5}
\]
For completeness, this follows inductively from Pascal's identity. It is true at \(k=0\). For \(0\le k<p-1\), the binomial coefficient \(\binom p{k+1}\) is divisible by \(p\), and
\[
0\equiv\binom p{k+1}
 =\binom{p-1}{k}+\binom{p-1}{k+1}.
\]
Thus each successive value is the negative of the preceding one, proving (5).

## 2. The values at \(p-1\)

We first evaluate \(a(p-1)\). By (5),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, this alternating sum of \(p\) terms is \(1\). Hence
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.                                                       \tag{6}
\]

Now put
\[
q=\frac{p-1}{2},
\]
so that \(2q=p-1\). We claim
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^q.                                                  \tag{7}
\]
Consider a term indexed by \(k\) in the defining sum for \(c(p-1)\). If \(k>q\), then \(p\le 2k\) and \(k<p\), so (3) gives
\(\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0\). If \(k<q\), set \(r=p-1-k\). Then \(r>q\), hence \(p\le2r\), while \(r<p\); consequently (3) gives
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=\binom{2r}{r}\equiv0.
\]
Thus every term except the one with \(k=q\) vanishes modulo \(p\).

For that remaining term, (5), together with \(2q=p-1\), gives
\[
\binom{p-1}{q}\equiv(-1)^q,
\qquad
\binom{2q}{q}=\binom{p-1}{q}\equiv(-1)^q.
\]
Both central binomial factors in the term are the latter coefficient. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
c(p-1)
&\equiv (-1)^q
 \bigl((-1)^q\bigr)^2
 \bigl((-1)^q\bigr)^2\\
&=(-1)^{5q}=(-1)^q,
\end{aligned}
\]
because the two squared factors are each \(1\). This proves (7).

## 3. Vanishing on the upper half of the Hankel matrices

We next prove that, for every integer \(m\) satisfying
\[
0\le m\le p-2,
\]
one has
\[
a(p+m)\equiv0,
\qquad
c(p+m)\equiv0.                                                       \tag{8}
\]
The inequality \(m\le p-2\) in particular gives \(m<p\).

### Vanishing of \(a(p+m)\)

Split the defining sum at \(p\): every index \(k\) between \(0\) and \(p+m\) is either \(k<p\), or uniquely has the form \(k=p+x\) with \(0\le x\le m\).

For \(0\le k<p\), congruence (1) gives
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk.
\]
If \(k>m\), the coefficient on the right is zero. Hence the entire part with \(k<p\) reduces to
\[
S:=\sum_{x=0}^m(-1)^x\binom mx^4.                                   \tag{9}
\]
For the remaining indices \(k=p+x\), where \(0\le x\le m\), congruence (2) gives
\[
\binom{p+m}{p+x}\equiv\binom mx.
\]
Moreover, since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x.
\]
Thus the contribution from these indices is
\[
-\sum_{x=0}^m(-1)^x\binom mx^4=-S.
\]
The two portions cancel term by term, proving \(a(p+m)\equiv0\).

### Vanishing of \(c(p+m)\)

We split the sum for \(c(p+m)\) in the same way. First take \(0\le k<p\). By (1),
\[
\binom{p+m}{k}\equiv\binom mk,
\]
so all terms with \(k>m\) vanish. For \(0\le k\le m\), write
\[
p+m-k=p+(m-k).
\]
Using (4) with \(r=m-k\), we obtain
\[
\binom{2(p+m-k)}{p+m-k}
\equiv 2\binom{2(m-k)}{m-k}.
\]
Consequently, the contribution of all indices below \(p\) is
\[
T:=\sum_{x=0}^m(-1)^x\binom mx^2\binom{2x}{x}
        \left(2\binom{2(m-x)}{m-x}\right).                            \tag{10}
\]

Now let \(k=p+x\), with \(0\le x\le m\). We have, successively,
\[
\binom{p+m}{p+x}\equiv\binom mx                                     \tag{11}
\]
by (2),
\[
\binom{2(p+x)}{p+x}\equiv2\binom{2x}{x}                              \tag{12}
\]
by (4), and
\[
p+m-(p+x)=m-x.                                                       \tag{13}
\]
The last central binomial factor is therefore simply
\(\binom{2(m-x)}{m-x}\). Also \((-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x\). Thus the term indexed by \(p+x\) is
\[
-(-1)^x\binom mx^2
 \left(2\binom{2x}{x}\right)
 \binom{2(m-x)}{m-x}.
\]
By commutativity of multiplication, this is exactly the negative of the term indexed by \(x\) in (10). Summing over \(x=0,\ldots,m\), the contribution from the indices at least \(p\) is \(-T\). Hence \(c(p+m)\equiv0\), completing the proof of (8).

Equivalently, (8) says that for either \(g(n)=a(n)\bmod p\) or \(g(n)=c(n)\bmod p\),
\[
g(n)=0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2).                                       \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, any such \(n\) can be written as \(n=p+m\) with \(0\le m\le p-2\).

## 4. A determinant lemma

We now evaluate a general Hankel determinant having the vanishing property (14). Let \(g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb F_p\) satisfy
\[
g(n)=0\quad\text{for }p\le n\le2p-2,
\]
and form the \(p\times p\) matrix
\[
M=(g(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Reverse the order of its columns. Denote the resulting matrix by \(B\). Its entries are
\[
B_{ij}=g\bigl(i+(p-1-j)\bigr).
\]
If \(i>j\), then
\[
p\le i+p-1-j\le2p-2,
\]
so \(B_{ij}=0\). Thus \(B\) is upper triangular. On the diagonal,
\[
B_{ii}=g(p-1),
\]
so
\[
\det B=g(p-1)^p.                                                      \tag{15}
\]
Fermat's identity \(x^p=x\) in \(\mathbb F_p\) turns this into
\[
\det B=g(p-1).                                                       \tag{16}
\]

It remains to account for the sign of the column reversal. The reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair of distinct positions, hence
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\mathrm{rev})=(-1)^{\binom p2}
=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Writing \(q=(p-1)/2\), and using the oddness of \(p\), the parity of \(pq\) is the parity of \(q\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\mathrm{rev})=(-1)^q.                             \tag{17}
\]
Column reversal changes a determinant by this sign, so
\[
\det B=(-1)^q\det M.
\]
Since \(((-1)^q)^2=1\), equations (16) and (17) give the general formula
\[
\det M=(-1)^q g(p-1).                                                \tag{18}
\]

## 5. Evaluation of the two determinants

Reduce the integer matrix
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\]
entrywise modulo \(p\). Reduction modulo \(p\) commutes with the determinant, since the determinant is an integer polynomial in the matrix entries. By (8), its associated function \(g(n)=a(n)\bmod p\) satisfies the hypothesis of (18), while (6) gives \(g(p-1)=1\). Hence
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^q\cdot1=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]

Similarly, reduce
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
\]
modulo \(p\). Again (8) supplies the required vanishing, and (7) gives
\[
g(p-1)=c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^q.
\]
Applying (18),
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^q(-1)^q=(-1)^{2q}=1\pmod p.
\]

Thus, for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p},
\]
as claimed.
